summary: The Headless Experience Layer (HXL), part of the Headless Toolkit in AIforce, lets you define an interactive widget once in declarative JSON and render it natively in Agentforce and in MCP clients that support MCP Apps, such as Claude and ChatGPT.

HXL has three core concepts: Components (surface-aware UI primitives), Widgets (composed experiences, stored as a UiWidgetBundle under uiWidgets/<name>/ with a .uiwidget-meta.xml, a composition JSON, and an optional schema.json), and Custom Lightning Types (CLTs) that bind data shape to a widget through renderer.json.

Widgets are not LWC or React and contain no JavaScript. They use {!$attrs.x} placeholders and forEach/forItem for lists, and the data comes from an Apex invocable action, so existing sharing and field-level security still apply.

Agentforce needs one CLT typed to the Apex class, and the Agent Script output must set complex_data_type_name and is_displayable: True. MCP needs two nested CLTs (inner mirrors the Apex output, outer mirrors the actionName/isSuccess/outputValues envelope) with paths like {!$attrs.outputValues.reviews.averageRating}, plus a uiResource on the MCP server tool definition.

The beta supports two client actions, sendMessage and openLink. Agentforce may sometimes return follow-up answers as text instead of the card, so name the action explicitly in the subagent instructions. The HXL Playground previews can differ from live surfaces, so test on each target.

summary: Native Data 360 chunking (section-aware, semantic passage extraction) works for clean content but breaks down on dense tables, multispeaker transcripts, and PII-laden documents in complex PDFs.

Data 360 Code Extension functions let you deploy sandboxed, stateless Python chunking scripts inside the Salesforce trust boundary, authored locally with the Data Custom Code SDK, deployed via Salesforce CLI or UI, and wired in at search index creation.

For tables, a structure-aware function detects markdown, grid and HTML tables, keeps each as a unit, and repeats column headers in every sub-chunk when a table exceeds the size limit; in the example, the agent went from being unable to interpret '42.1 35.8 22.4...' to correctly reporting 87.9% YoY growth and a 28.1% operating margin for AI & Automation.

For multispeaker dialogue, a sliding window (WINDOW_SIZE=6 turns, STRIDE=3, MAX_CHUNK_CHARS=1500) preserves speaker attribution and timestamps and keeps questions co-located with answers, fixing native chunks where speakers and topics were mashed together.

Caveat from the author: the sample code relies on regex heuristics, covers only happy-path inputs, and can produce false positives and negatives, so production use needs hardening; the post also covers a third use case, masking exposed PII, though the provided text is truncated before it.

summary: The post introduces /decide, a structured skill in the open-source Salesforce Ada Agent Skills repo. It makes a coding agent run a technical decision through a pipeline and write the result to disk as an Architectural Decision Record (ADR).

The pipeline has five steps: gather context, list solution options from official docs, define evaluation criteria, assess risk per option (Low/Medium/High with citations), and compute a decision score. The human reviews and confirms after the options, criteria and risk steps, and the agent pauses at each of these checkpoints.

Scoring is rule-based. Risk levels map to fixed values (Low=85, Medium=55, High=25), which are weighted by Well-Architected pillars: Reliability 20%, Stability 20%, Operational Excellence 20%, Resource Optimization 15%, Cost Optimization 15%, Fairness 10%. The highest score is always the recommendation.

Design patterns include a folder layout with CLAUDE.md global rules plus SKILL.md pipeline logic, separate format template files per step, and a roughly 350-line scoring file loaded only at the final step. Critical rules are repeated in at least two files so they survive long conversations.

Facts are checked against docs via an MCP server. The authors built a custom salesforce-content server with keyword and vector search, the repo includes a Context7 fallback, and the skill falls back to web search or model knowledge if no MCP is available. The skill is demonstrated with Claude Code, and the repo has templates for Gemini and Codex CLI.

summary: The post advises admins to pick a small first Agentforce use case: one recurring problem for one user group, with one clear job and a measurable outcome.

Listen for friction signals such as "I can never find…" or "Can you summarize this for me?". Users who export Salesforce data into unapproved consumer AI tools are a strong sign of unmet need and a data-handling risk that a governed Agentforce experience could replace.
Keep a friction log for at least a week, recording the goal, what slowed users down, the workaround, how often it happens, and what a better outcome looks like.

First check whether Agentforce is the right tool, meaning the job needs natural-language interpretation, summarization, context, or next-step decisions. Otherwise use something like Flow. Then score the remaining criteria from 1 to 5: data readiness (weighted most heavily), business value, frequency, manageable risk, and measurable outcome.

For implementation, use a standard action where one exists (for example Summarize Record, which uses a Record Summary prompt template). Otherwise build a custom action powered by a prompt template (tailored generative output) or by Flow (deterministic processes). Combining Agentforce for interpretation with Flow for approved steps often works best.

summary: Skye Tyler (Principal Solution Consultant, Beyond the Horizon Technology) argues that clean metadata is essential for reliable AI agents, comparing agents to an enthusiastic intern with short-term memory problems.

Recommended approach is 'clean-as-you-go': whenever you update an object or build a new AI-enabled business process, review and update descriptions and help text for the related fields the agent can touch.

summary: Voice-enabling an Agent Script agent is not a rewrite: you enable Agentforce Voice in the org, add three voice blocks to the script, and retune the instructions for listeners.

The org must have Agentforce Voice turned on (it runs on Salesforce Voice with Telephony Providers). You can check by searching for Telephony under Add Connections in Agentforce Builder, and a free Developer Edition org currently doesn't support it.

The three required script blocks are a top-level `language` (default_locale), `connection telephony` (which makes it a voice agent), and `modality voice` (outbound persona_id and model.id, inbound filler_words_detection).
`language` must appear both at the top level and inside `modality voice`, because the persona_id resolves against a model and language and otherwise silently falls back to the default voice.

Supported voice models are eleven_v3_conversational, eleven_flash_v2_5, eleven_flash_v2 (English only) and kotoba (Japanese). The model can only be set in Script view, and the legacy flat voice_id format cannot pick a model.

summary: Salesforce Microfrontend (UI Embedding), currently Beta and tested on a Winter '27 Preview scratch org (API 68.0), lets a React UI Bundle from Multi-Framework be embedded in Lightning Experience record pages via `lightning-ui-embedding`.

Embedding needs a thin wrapper LWC that passes the app's `*.salesforce.app` URL as `src` to `<lightning-ui-embedding>`. The app URL must also be registered under Setup > Trusted URLs with the `frame-src` CSP context enabled.

`recordId` did not arrive in `state.props`, which was empty on the record page. The reliable route was custom events on the `sf-embedding` channel: the LWC dispatches `caseRecordId` and the app dispatches `requestRecordId`.

Waiting only for `sf-embedding.component.ready` dropped the event, because the app registers its listener after `createViewSDK()` resolves. A handshake fixed this: the app registers its listener and then requests the recordId, and the LWC replies on either `ready` or the request.

Two other pitfalls: keep `src` as a fixed base URL after mount, and avoid `100vh`/`min-h-screen` inside the iframe, which makes the auto-resizer grow the iframe without end. The post suggests using `height:auto` instead, and the LWC height is a design attribute clamped to 420–720px.

summary: Agentforce Vibes has a new feature called Abilities, which automatically picks the Salesforce DX MCP Server tools that fit a developer's intent. Developers no longer need to hand-pick tools or switch modes.

The problem it addresses: more than 80 DX MCP tools are available, but enabling all of them bloats prompts, hurts output quality and raises token cost. Only a default subset is on, and customizing it means hand-editing the local mcp_config.json with internal tool names.

Abilities are domain-specific capability groups, such as Apex and LWC development, DevOps operations, mobile development and core platform management. An internal Ability Coordinator evaluates each prompt and prepares the toolset before the model is called. Abilities can combine within one request.

Tool selection uses RAG-based semantic search in three phases. Tool definitions (name, description, parameters, usage context) are embedded and stored in a vector database. The prompt is embedded with the same model and matched by cosine similarity, typically returning about 10 tools. Those tools are then injected into the model's context as a temporary function catalog.

Orchestrator tools often need helper tools that the search may not return, so Abilities add dependent tools after selection. Skills are separate: Abilities decide which tools are available, while Skills define reusable task workflows (e.g. refactoring triggers, generating tests, deploying).

summary: Salesforce Hosted MCP Server security is built in layers: authentication, authorization, permission control (object/field level), and logging for audit.

Authentication supports only the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow through an External Client App (ECA). Shared service or integration-user sessions are called an anti-pattern, and machine-to-machine flows are not planned.
A dedicated ECA per MCP client (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor) is strongly recommended. The new `mcp_api` OAuth scope grants MCP server access without the broad `api` scope.

Authorization controls include restricting ECA access to approved profiles or permission sets (for example an "MCP Client User" permission set), trusted IP ranges, and a shorter refresh token lifetime (the default is 1 year). Tokens can be revoked in Setup under OAuth Usage.

All MCP servers are disabled by default, so enable only the ones you want to expose. Tool annotations (for example destructive or idempotent hints) help agents behave safely, but clients are not required to honor them.

summary: The Headless Experience Layer (HXL), announced at TDX 2026, entered beta in August 2026 and lets Salesforce data appear as rich custom UI widgets in external AI agent apps such as Slackbot, ChatGPT and Claude.

The post builds an account opportunity summary widget in 7 steps: an Apex invocable class, LightningTypes with a renderer, a UiWidgetBundle, a GenAiFunction, a McpServerDefinition, deployment, and enabling the MCP server and connecting from an agent app.
Data flows through two separate paths: tools (the Apex action, registered through GenAiFunction in the API catalog) and resources (the widget UI), and McpServerDefinition ties them together.

The MCP response is a 3-layer envelope (Result → OutputValues → Apex Summary), and renderer.json maps values into widget attributes with expressions like {!$attrs.outputValues.summary.accountName}. A wrong path depth means nothing displays.

Widgets are built as JSON trees of tile/* components (row, column, avatar, badge, text, icon). Using a nonexistent tile/icon name such as 'currency' crashes the whole widget with a NullPointerException and only a generic 'unexpected error' message; 'briefcase' and 'dollar-sign' work.

summary: This is the second post in a series on LWC anti-patterns; it covers the @wire service, public @api properties, and event handling, following a first post on security and Lightning Web Security.

The central mental model is that @wire is a subscription, not a one-time fetch. Adapters can emit multiple times (cache, network, other components' edits), so handlers must be idempotent and derive all state from the latest emission.

Wire data is immutable, so copy it into a local property before mutating. Never change wire config inside renderedCallback(), which causes an infinite render loop. Don't assume multiple adapters fire in order, and don't read wire data in connectedCallback().

For LDS caching, use notifyRecordUpdateAvailable() after imperative Apex writes instead of refreshApex(), which is deprecated for LDS adapters like getRecord. Don't mix Apex and LDS for the same record, and don't add dummy optionalFields to bust the cache.

Other wire fixes: import field tokens from @salesforce/schema, use full relationship paths such as Case.Account.Name in getRecord, and gate dependent data with undefined reactive properties instead of promise chains. Use top-level '$prop' config values instead of swapping a config object, and use imperative Apex rather than @wire for DML.

summary: The post shows how Agentforce agents can call external MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools over JSON-RPC via HTTP, with no custom Apex callouts or middleware.

In Agent Studio you create an Agentforce Employee Agent with a subagent, add the MCP tools from the Asset Library, then commit and activate the version and test it in Preview (e.g. 'What is the current time in New Delhi?'). Salesforce handles token caching and refresh, retries and error handling.

Keep a mix of preview and non-preview sandboxes during the roughly four-week preview window. Dev, integration, and UAT sandboxes that form the deployment path should stay non-preview, refreshed if they were slated to move to preview.

Deploy from like states (non-preview sandbox to non-preview sandbox to non-preview Production). Avoid deploying from a preview sandbox into non-preview Production: new-release metadata such as new permissions can make the deployment fail, and Git doesn't track the release version, so source control won't catch it.

Check a sandbox's state with the Sandboxes page's Location column plus the Salesforce Sandbox Preview Guide. To handle the 600+ page Release Notes, have an AI tool condense them and show which sections it skipped, then verify its judgment yourself.

tasks.title: Audit sandboxes in Setup and the Sandbox Preview Guide, and mark each as preview or non-preview, with the dev/UAT deployment path kept non-preview
Review pending Release Updates in Setup and test those nearing enforcement in a sandbox

summary: The post is an admin-focused guide to Winter '27 highlights, with the reminder that the 600+ page release notes don't need to be read in full, and it explains pilot, beta and GA feature phases.
Two new User Interface Settings (off by default) allow list view inline editing of any field the user can access, even if it isn't on the page layout, and across lists with multiple record types.
User Field History Tracking is now GA and auto-enabled, tracking up to 20 User fields with data retained for up to 18 months in the UI.

A new 'Keep manual shares when transferring records' sharing setting stops Salesforce from deleting manual shares on owner change, and Custom Row Causes for standard objects via Metadata API are targeted for October 10, with Setup management by early November (forward-looking).

Email and MFA updates include a User Email Domains page, importing authorized email domains into sandboxes from production, per-domain verification rules (Always, For Updated Addresses Only, Never), and Chrome extension entries (`chromeextension://[32-char-id]`, no wildcards) in Trusted URLs.

tasks.title: Enable User Field History Tracking and the 'Keep manual shares when transferring records' setting in a sandbox, then test a record owner transfer
Review User Email Domains and Authorized Email Domains in Setup, and configure 'Allow copy to sandbox' for production domains

summary: Flow Test Mode (Beta) is a dedicated testing workspace that replaces the Debug button in Flow Builder and merges debugging and automated testing into one experience.
Debug runs can be saved as named manual test scenarios that keep the triggering record, input variables, and mocked outputs, so they can be reused or shared with coworkers.
Saved scenarios can be turned into permanent regression tests by adding assertions (expected results), using Apex test classes to create isolated test data for each test.

New inputs include static 15- or 18-character record IDs (useful for Cases, Campaign Members, Content Document, and Setup objects) and primitive collections, which can be entered as a semicolon-delimited list.

Subflow and action outputs can be mocked, for example to fake an HTTP callout response, and flow coverage visualization on the canvas arrives in Winter '27 along with Agentforce for Flow Headless test generation.

tasks.title: Enable Flow Test Mode (Beta) in a sandbox or scratch org and save two manual test scenarios on a record-triggered flow
Convert a saved scenario into an automated regression test with assertions and mock an HTTP callout action, then check whether deployment to another org requires the beta setting

summary: The September Monthly Retro podcast episode with Joshua Birk and Kate Lessard recaps Dreamforce 2026 from an admin's perspective.

Builder Central is a low-code/no-code AI workspace for building React sites, flows, agents, data models and permissions from plain-language prompts, with automated testing, safety checks and built-in controls.

Admins can upload requirements documents and business-process information to Builder Central so it builds against their actual data model and org structure; the hosts stress testing in a sandbox and "trust but verify".
Headless 360 and the Headless Experience Layer let Salesforce surface in Slack, Claude and other interfaces; the keynote demoed running an auto-launched case-escalation flow directly from Claude.

The main Dreamforce takeaway is that governance and trust matter more, so admins should focus on data cleanup and strict permissions, and on tracking how data moves across platforms and who can access it; new tools include Security Center Essentials and the Transaction Security Policy Accelerator.

tasks.title: Try Builder Central in a sandbox with a requirements doc and check the generated flow or data model against your org
Evaluate the Transaction Security Policy Accelerator and Security Center Essentials in a sandbox and compare them with your current security policies

summary: Agentforce Vibes opens from Setup as a cloud-hosted Visual Studio Code instance configured for your org, so admins work in a virtualized environment rather than directly in the org.

Skills are packaged instructions for distinct tasks, such as creating objects, adding fields or validation rules, and deploying metadata. Vibes picks the matching skill from the verbs in your prompt, which avoids guessing and wasting tokens.

A library of Salesforce and Trailblazer Community skills now comes pre-installed. Find them under Toolkit > Skills, add more with + Add Skill, or get them from the GitHub repo forcedotcom/afv-library.

Plan mode shows a plan for approval before Vibes executes anything. All changes stay on Vibes' own filesystem until you explicitly ask it to deploy, so you should try it in a Developer Edition, scratch org or sandbox.

In the author's example, a prompt to build a report of active system administrators led to a deploy that initially failed because Vibes guessed the wrong report type. It then retried with other APIs, and the author warns that technical errors such as access tokens may appear along the way.

tasks.title: In a sandbox or scratch org, open Agentforce Vibes, set up a Standard project, and use Plan mode to create and deploy a report from a prompt
Browse the pre-installed skills in Toolkit > Skills and the forcedotcom/afv-library repo, then try a permission set or record-triggered flow skill in a sandbox

summary: Builder Central is a new no-code, AI-powered workspace for building apps, agents, and experiences from natural language. It enters beta the week after Dreamforce for orgs with Agentforce enabled, and every org gets it free with usage limits.
Salesforce Quick Pages lets admins and permissioned users build single-page React apps on top of existing data without putting org metadata at risk.
Agentforce Coworker is an out-of-the-box autonomous assistant in Lightning that respects the logged-in user's permissions. Admins can set it up in under 5 minutes.

The Headless Experience Layer (HXL) lets admins build deterministic UI widgets tied to data, automation, and business logic that work across every interface. The HXL Playground is available to try now.
Security Center Essentials is a free dashboard for security posture, enabled by assigning the View Security Center Pages permission, with no support case needed.

tasks.title: Assign View Security Center Pages permission and review the Security Center Essentials dashboard in a sandbox
Install the Transaction Security Policy Accelerator from AgentExchange in a sandbox and evaluate prebuilt policies against current TSPs

summary: Before building an Agentforce agent, the post argues you should fix your metadata first, because field labels, API names and descriptions are the context the agent uses to understand your data.
The review starts by scoping to the objects, fields and flows one agent use case touches, such as the 23-field Opportunity object, rather than cleaning the whole org.

Agentforce Vibes IDE is opened from Setup (gear icon, then Agentforce Vibes) in a Developer Edition org. A first prompt in non-Plan mode pulls the Opportunity field metadata into a table that can be downloaded as CSV or Markdown.

A second prompt, run in Plan mode and explicitly told not to make changes, flags custom fields whose label, API name and description describe different concepts or whose descriptions are missing or ambiguous. For each one it shows evidence and, where the evidence supports it, a draft description. In the author's test it flagged five custom fields and drafted good descriptions for three.

After you review the drafts and click Approve Plan, Vibes updates the field descriptions and summarizes the changes. Fields it couldn't describe (OrderNumber__c, TrackingNumber__c, Stage_1__c to Stage_4__c) go to the business for answers, and those answers can be applied by attaching a CSV to the chat or with a one-line prompt.

tasks.title: In a Developer Edition org, run the Agentforce Vibes metadata-pull and Plan-mode gap-review prompts against a custom or Opportunity object and approve the drafted field descriptions
Pick one planned agent use case, list its objects, fields and flows, and use Vibes to audit the custom field descriptions in a sandbox, then send the unresolved fields to the business owners as a CSV

summary: Security Center Essentials is now fully rolled out to production orgs and some sandboxes, extending Health Check's point-in-time configuration score with ongoing visibility into an org's security posture.

It currently surfaces seven metrics, including installed managed packages, connected apps and third-party access, trusted IP ranges, who installed what, and recent changes; this is planned to expand to 14 metrics by Dreamforce.

Sabrina Simeroth recommends two review questions: what should be in my environment (owner, installer, users of each package), and what changed most recently (expected or not, by whom, and the impact on business processes).
Admins should set a monitoring cadence tied to business milestones, such as checking before and after a weekly Tuesday update, and escalate anything unexpected to the security and governance team.
A perfect Health Check score shouldn't be the goal: it should start a security review rather than end one, and any gaps you accept should be known, intentional risks.

tasks.title: Open Security Center Essentials in a production or sandbox org and inventory managed packages, connected apps, and trusted IP ranges, noting owner and installer for each
Run Health Check, document any intentional deviations from the baseline, and set up a recurring review cadence tied to your release or update schedule

summary: Security Center Essentials is a free, centralized org security dashboard for admins that is generally available now and needs no support case to enable.
The dashboard shows a Health Check Score measured against the Salesforce baseline or a custom baseline you define.
It keeps 30 days of metric history so you can track improvements and regressions, and use it as evidence of progress for leadership.
Core metrics shown in one place include connected apps, installed packages, login IP ranges, and trusted IP ranges.
To enable it, assign the 'View Security Center Pages' permission, then open it from the App Launcher or Setup.

tasks.title: Assign View Security Center Pages to yourself in a sandbox or prod org and review the Health Check Score against the Salesforce baseline
Audit connected apps and trusted IP ranges in Security Center Essentials and list stale or unapproved items to remove

summary: Salesforce channels create a dedicated Slack channel for a Salesforce record (Accounts, Opportunities, Cases, Campaigns, or custom objects), so conversations stay tied to CRM data.

Setup is in Setup > Slack Channels for Records: enable Show Slack Button on Selected Objects, pick objects (Accounts, Opportunities and Cases are suggested starting points), and add them via Add Objects if needed.
Admins then add the Slack component to Lightning record pages in Lightning App Builder and activate the page as Org Default, App Default, or by App, Record Type, or Profile.
Default channel preferences, set from the Slack organization's settings, cover channel name, channel privacy, and which related lists show in the channel.
Slackbot can summarize a record (e.g. 'Catch me up on the Acme account'), create or update Salesforce records, and answer questions from Salesforce data and Slack conversations.

tasks.title: Enable Salesforce channels for Account in a sandbox, add the Slack component to the Account record page, and create a test record channel
Draft a channel naming convention and pilot plan for Accounts, Opportunities and Cases, and try Slackbot record summaries and updates in the pilot channels

summary: A single do-everything agent gets hard to maintain because subagents (formerly topics) compete for the same requests and the reasoning engine makes surprising choices.
The recommended pattern is a Super Agent that owns the user conversation and delegates to Connected Subagents, with each one decomposed by functional domain, workflow stage, or capability.

Use a Connected Subagent where work hands off to a different team or system and the task has its own input and output plus enough reasoning and data access. If it's a single step with no real reasoning, make it an action instead.

Keep the Super Agent's instructions focused on routing, and put cross-cutting concerns there: guardrails and compliance (e.g. GDPR opt-out), one-time user verification and context priming, disambiguation, and human handoff.

In the author's Pronto Delivery Concierge build, description-based routing was right only about 80% of the time, so they added a deterministic Agent Script conditional (if @variables.order_status == "In Progress": invoke @actions.go_to_Logistics_Dispatch) after a Get Order Details flow action.

tasks.title: Build a Super Agent in a sandbox with two Connected Subagents and add an order_status conditional that overrides description-based routing
Audit existing Agentforce subagent descriptions for vague or overlapping wording and apply the one-sentence 'no and' test

summary: Dedicated, system-generated test data makes flow tests predictable, because tests no longer depend on records that may be deleted, changed, or missing in another org.
Flow tests that rely on org data break when the chosen record changes or when a flow version moves to a data-dry sandbox or Developer Edition org.
Test data comes from an Apex class that is annotated @isTest, has a method annotated @testSetup, and is declared global so the flow testing UI can see it.
The data is ephemeral: it exists only while the test runs and is never written to the data layer, so you can create, update, and delete records freely.

Admins should give developers a brief on the flow's purpose, the trigger record and fields, related records, and the data volume needed (for example 500 records instead of 5), then attach the class on the flow test's Test Setup tab.

tasks.title: Write a global @isTest class with a @testSetup method for a simple flow, deploy it to a scratch org, and attach it on the flow test's Test Setup tab
Audit existing flow tests for dependence on specific org records and list candidates to move to dedicated Apex test data

summary: Pairing a boolean toggle (e.g., tgl_update_client) with the Read Only and Disabled settings on Screen Flow components lets you capture user intent, not just the final field values.

A boolean formula resource that inverts the toggle (True when the toggle is off) is applied to the Read Only or Disabled setting on every field, so fields stay locked until the user turns the toggle on.
The toggle's own Disabled setting is set to tgl_update_client.value, so once it's on it can't be switched off. This stops users from thinking they need to uncheck it to 'lock in' their edits.
Read Only fields still allow highlighting and copying text, while Disabled fields are grayed out and block copy-paste. Static booleans can permanently lock fields such as name and date of birth.

Caveat: toggles aren't always initialized to False, so a skipped screen or conditional visibility can leave the value null, and writing null to a checkbox field errors. Set it to False in an Assignment element before the record update.

tasks.title: Build a scratch-org Screen Flow with a toggle, an inverse formula resource, and Read Only/Disabled fields, then write the toggle to a checkbox field
Audit existing Screen Flows that pre-populate record data and add 'section changed' toggles, with an Assignment element to default them to False

summary: Michelle Wolfe, a Platform Engineer, built a no-code, Flow-powered user management system that handles requests, approvals, user creation, permissions, communications and onboarding.
The problem was onboarding classes of 80+ new hires, where managers emailed individual members of a three-person admin team who then created each account by hand.
A screen flow now collects the request details and creates a case, which centralizes intake and lets the team track productivity, due dates and workload.

After the manager approves, an autolaunched flow validates the data, creates the alias and username, and sets the profile and permissions from the request. A second autolaunched flow closes the case and sends a confirmation email and a welcome email.
She replaced Add Multiple Users and bulk upload because Add Multiple Users doesn't support custom fields, so records failed her validation rules, and bulk upload broke on typos.

tasks.title: Prototype a screen flow in a scratch org that captures new-user request details (including a custom Team Name field) and creates a Case
Build an approval-triggered autolaunched flow that creates a User with a generated alias and username and assigns a profile and permission set

summary: The post is an admin countdown of key dates for the Winter '27 Salesforce release.
August 13: admins can sign up for a pre-release Developer Edition org with all Winter '27 features, and anyone with a Summer '26 pre-release org can log back into it.
August 19: Release Notes are published in Salesforce Help, and the Release Readiness Trailblazer Community Group offers community breakdowns and Q&A.

August 27 before 5 p.m. PT is the deadline to refresh a sandbox that is not slated for preview, using the Sandbox Preview Guide, and sandbox preview begins August 28 (the post also mentions a January 8 deadline, which looks inconsistent with the August dates).

Winter '27 reaches production on September 4, October 2 and October 9, depending on the instance, so check the Maintenance Calendar and Release Updates in Setup, and look for Admin Evangelist Jen's Be Release Ready blog on October 5.

tasks.title: Sign up for a Winter '27 pre-release Developer Edition org and test key customizations
Check the Sandbox Preview Guide for your sandbox instances and refresh before the deadline if needed, then review Release Updates in Setup

summary: The October 2026 B2C Commerce release makes the SCAPI zone (the eCDN zone in front of Commerce API traffic) manageable in Business Manager and the CDN API. One zone is shared across Dev, Staging, and Production and is managed from Production only.

The SCAPI zone supports custom firewall rules, rate limiting, IP access lists, analytics, and cache purge. It does not support WAF managed rulesets, mTLS, TLS 1.3 settings, HSTS, Page Shield, or Under Attack Mode, and the Crypto tab is read-only.

The new SCAPI Identity Header (SIH) lets you accept Shopper API traffic only from Managed Runtime. Enable the Managed Runtime SCAPI Request Identification feature per instance, then add a custom block rule on the instance's path segment (e.g. f_ecom_abcd_prd plus /shopper) after the locked managed allow rule. Start in Log mode before switching to Block.

Custom BFFs, mobile backends, and partner integrations can't present the SIH, so each needs its own allow rule with a server-side shared-secret header, placed above the block rule. SLAS hardening: Strict Client Auth requires an x-slas-client-auth header for private clients, but PWA Kit and Storefront Next don't send it yet, so enabling it for those clients breaks shopper login with 401s. SLAS also throttles refresh-token exchanges to 3 per 60 seconds, returning a 429 beyond that.

Two new fields work on every eCDN zone: Known Bot (cf.client.bot) and Verified Bot Category (cf.verified_bot_category, 17 categories such as AI Crawler, AI Search, AI Assistant, and Search Engine Crawler). Use them to rate limit AI traffic on expensive endpoints like product search (example: 30 requests per 60 seconds per IP, log first). They cover only Cloudflare-verified bots, so unverified or spoofed automation needs bot scores or a third-party bot manager.

tasks.title: Audit which API clients call Shopper API directly (BFFs, mobile, partners) and map them to needed SIH allow rules
Create a Log-mode custom firewall rule on the SCAPI zone for direct /shopper traffic and review Security Analytics matches before enforcing
Add a Log-mode rate limiting rule for AI Crawler and AI Search categories on product-search and review thresholds against real traffic

summary: The post introduces a new AI extensibility stack for admins under AIforce: MCPs (Model Context Protocol), Skills, and Plugins.

MCP is a standardized layer over APIs that lets AI securely fetch live context or take action, such as querying CRM records, searching records, or triggering auto-launched flows. Skills define repeatable steps, rules, and formatting for a task. Plugins bundle MCP connectors, skills, and interfaces for one-click install.

The post lists new admin skills: MCP management (including external client applications and Agentic Identity), agent skills and Super Agent orchestration with subagents, plugin lifecycle management mapped to user roles, Agentforce Coworker setup, and Agent Script.

Agent Script uses hybrid reasoning to define guardrails, tone, required steps, and logic declaratively in Agentforce Studio. Builder Central and Agentforce Vibes provide AI-assisted building, but admins still need solid fundamentals like schema, layouts, and permissions.

The suggested roadmap runs from the AI Trust, Security, and Governance trail (Agentblazer Champion), to Coworker and Studio (Innovator), to Builder Central, Vibes, and plugin packaging (Legend), then to change management.

tasks.title: Set up Agentforce Coworker in a sandbox and test which skills and MCPs surface in global search, Slack, and mobile
Document a central inventory of org-wide MCP connections and external client apps, with the permissions each one needs

summary: This is the third post in the LWC anti-patterns series. It covers DOM access, async timing, lifecycle hooks, performance, and base component usage.

Don't use document.querySelector, innerHTML, or #id selectors, because LWC rewrites ids and scopes shadow DOM. Use this.template.querySelector or lwc:ref (this.refs.x) instead, and use lightning-formatted-rich-text for trusted rich HTML.
Don't use setTimeout to wait for data or re-renders. Use async/await for data, and use renderedCallback() with a guard flag for DOM work, since it fires after every render.

Don't read @api properties or touch the DOM in constructor() or connectedCallback(), because values and children aren't ready yet. Use connectedCallback, @wire, or renderedCallback, and avoid this.template.children.
Under Lightning Web Security, clone Apex/LDS data once on arrival before looping, and prefer plain objects and arrays over Set/Map for large collections.

tasks.title: Run the LWC ESLint plugin (including no-inner-html) over your repo and fix flagged document.querySelector, innerHTML, and #id selector usage
Replace ShowToastEvent with lightning/toast in components used on LWR or Experience Cloud sites and verify toasts appear in a scratch org
Audit components for setTimeout-based waits and constructor/connectedCallback DOM or @api access, and refactor to renderedCallback, async/await, or @wire

summary: The Metadata Grounding MCP Server (Beta) lets coding agents search a pre-indexed catalog of an org's metadata by natural-language intent, so they find existing components before building new ones.

It exposes three read-only tools, describe_metadata, search_metadata and query_metadata, following a describe, search, then query pattern across 70+ metadata types such as objects, fields, LWCs, Apex classes, flows and permission sets.

It is backed by Salesforce Catalog on Data 360, using a hybrid vector and keyword index. Incremental sync covers supported types, and a full refresh runs every 24 hours, so recent deployments can lag.

Two Pronto examples show it in use: a vague menu-page bug led to MenuBrowserController and the c__menuBrowser LWC, and a review-summary request led to the existing AgentSummarizeReviewsActions class, which was extended instead of rebuilt.

It returns metadata and properties, not source code, and it is not an exhaustive inventory. Agents must retrieve code via the CLI or Metadata API and should confirm a record with query_metadata before coding against it.

tasks.title: Enable Salesforce Catalog in a sandbox, activate the Metadata Grounding MCP Server, and connect it to your coding agent (e.g. Claude Code)
Add the 'check the org first' project rule, or install the platform-metadata-grounding-get skill from sf-skills, and test it with a ticket for a feature you suspect already exists
Audit descriptions on key Apex classes and LWCs in your org to improve search ranking

summary: Builder Central is a new no-code beta experience that builds and deploys apps and agents from plain-language prompts in a single hub.
It already knows your existing orgs' configuration and security/permissions, so new apps and agents inherit those controls.
Unlike Setup with Agentforce, which makes direct changes such as creating a field, Builder Central targets complex builds like full data models, flows, and agents.
It complements rather than replaces Flow Builder, Lightning App Builder, and Agentforce Builder, and deploys through Lifecycle Center following your pipeline.

Safety features include interactive metadata visualizations (data model, agents, flows, pages, permission sets) and ephemeral preview orgs, which are temporary sandbox clones, so nothing touches sandbox or production until you publish.

tasks.title: Enable the Builder Central beta in a Developer sandbox (permission, beta toggle, Metadata Experts MCP Server) and build a small app from a prompt
Test the preview org and Lifecycle Center deployment flow, and review the generated metadata visualizations for permission set accuracy

summary: Quick Pages (Beta, Winter '27) lets users describe a page in natural language and an agent builds a React-based single-page app with live preview, using live org data (including custom objects and fields) with tiles, charts, tables and tabs.

It works on Lightning Experience Enterprise/Performance/Unlimited/Developer Edition orgs with Foundations on Hyperforce, and requires Multi-Framework Apps domain enabled, Salesforce Edge Network on, and Einstein turned on.

Setup is to toggle Quick Pages on in Setup, then assign the 'Create and View Quick Pages (Beta)' permission set to creators or 'View Quick Pages (Beta)' to viewers; no admin rights are needed to build pages.

Pages can be refined via chat or suggested 'NEXT' prompts (e.g. sorting, a phase filter dropdown), then saved and shared with individuals, public groups or the whole org, and viewers only see data they already have access to.

Beta caveats: pages are read-only (no create/update/delete), prompts over about 2 minutes time out, page names can't be changed after saving, Japanese IME Enter can send prematurely, there is no Apex/Connect REST/Data 360/external API access, and no packaging or data-export migration.

tasks.title: Enable Quick Pages in a fresh Developer Edition, assign the Create permission set, and build an opportunity dashboard
Run the sample-data Anonymous Apex script and iterate on the page with 3-4 chat refinements, noting timeouts and IME issues
Share a saved Quick Page with a user holding restricted permissions and verify they see only the data they can access

summary: The post shows how to build a Python agent with AWS's open-source Strands Agents SDK that reads Salesforce Cases through the Salesforce Hosted MCP Server, has an Amazon Bedrock model (Amazon Nova 2 Lite) judge priority, and writes the Priority field back without any Salesforce API code.

Setup: enable the sobject-reads and sobject-mutations servers under Setup > MCP Servers (up to 2 minutes to go live), then create an External Client App with the mcp_api and refresh_token/offline_access scopes and a localhost callback. The app can take up to 30 minutes to become usable.

Access is narrowed in four layers: the authorizing user's permissions, using sobject-mutations (which has no delete tool), Strands `tool_filters` limiting tools to soqlQuery and updateSobjectRecord, and an optional Strands Interrupts human-approval step that the post leaves out.
Authentication uses an OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE, handled by a small sf_auth.py script that stores the token at ~/.config with 0600 permissions and refreshes it after 60 minutes.

Caveats: Nova 2 reasoning must be enabled or the model sometimes skips the update tool call. The agent re-queries after updating to verify the writes. One run used about 10k input and 3.5k output tokens. Hosted MCP Server may incur Flex Credits charges, and it isn't available in orgs that lack the MCP Servers setup page.

tasks.title: Enable sobject-reads and sobject-mutations in a Developer Edition org, create the External Client App, and run sf_auth.py login to verify the PKCE flow
Build the Strands Agents + Bedrock case-triage agent against the BEDROCK-DEMO test Cases and confirm the Priority updates and the re-query check
Add a Strands Interrupts human-approval step before updateSobjectRecord and compare behavior with and without it

summary: The Headless Toolkit combines the Salesforce Skills Library (sf-skills, 250+ skills following the open Agent Skills spec), Hosted MCP Servers, and the Salesforce CLI so coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Agentforce Vibes can build, test, and deploy on Salesforce.

It proposes a seven-stage agent-driven loop (ground, specify, build, verify, review, release, observe), where each stage leaves a repo artifact such as a feature map, ontology.yaml, living spec, or review report, and each agent mistake feeds back into a new test, rule, or spec.

Grounding uses a feature map, a business-term ontology.yaml, and the read-only Metadata Grounding MCP Server (Beta), which needs Data 360, API access, and Salesforce Catalog, is unavailable in scratch orgs and namespaced Developer Edition orgs, and can lag on recent changes.

Hosted MCP Servers are off by default and must be enabled in Setup under MCP Servers (API Catalog), with activation taking up to two minutes; the author recommends spec-anchored specs for non-trivial work but skipping them for small fixes.

The author advises keeping context lean (deep work under roughly 300K tokens to avoid context rot) and using subagents, defined in .claude/agents/ with scoped skills and tools, only for substantial standalone work since each adds cost and latency.

tasks.title: Enable the Hosted MCP Servers in a sandbox or dev org via Setup > MCP Servers and install the salesforce-development plugin for Claude Code
Draft an ontology.yaml and a feature map for one business capability in your repo and reference them from AGENTS.md
Try the full loop on one multi-metadata feature: write a spec, build with a scoped subagent, then run an adversarial review pass and record what the harness missed

summary: Winter '27 (API version 68.0) adds two metadata types, AiAgentDefinition (agent-level settings) and AiAgentDefinitionVersion (one version, with an inline <planner> element holding subagents and actions), replacing the Bot, BotVersion and GenAiPlannerBundle split for Agentforce agents.

In the sample TestAgent (1 version, 10 subagents, 26 actions), all 37 generated-suffix names like ServiceCustomerVerification_1796152b9540575 disappear, and localDeveloperName becomes the name used for subagent-to-action links, so diffs between versions get much smaller.
Welcome, error and escalation dialogs collapse into three simple elements (welcomeMessage, errorMessage, escalationMessage), and Salesforce builds the dialogs on deploy.

The # member syntax selects versions (TestAgent#1, TestAgent#* for all versions of an agent, * for all agents), shrinking a hand-written manifest from 7 types and 14 members to 2 types, and AiAuthoringBundle folders always carry a version suffix such as TestAgent_1.

Caveats: at API 68.0, retrieving or deploying Agentforce agents as Bot or BotVersion errors out (Bot types are now for classic Einstein Bots, so stay on 67.0 to keep using them), and the # syntax plus --root-type-with-dependencies need Salesforce CLI 2.149.9 or later (run sf update).

tasks.title: Run sf update, then retrieve an existing agent at API 68.0 in a scratch org using TestAgent#* and compare the folder layout to the 67.0 retrieve
Rewrite my agent package.xml to the two-type AiAgentDefinition/AiAgentDefinitionVersion manifest and test sf project retrieve start with --root-type-with-dependencies AiAgentDefinitionVersion
Audit my CI/CD pipeline and scripts for hard-coded Bot, GenAiPlannerBundle or suffixed-name references that will break when moving to API 68.0

summary: Builder Central, now in beta, lets admins go from describing an idea to a working no-code solution on the platform using agent-powered tools.
It lets you build and preview work in a virtual environment before publishing to a sandbox, so you avoid making and rolling back metadata changes while iterating.
Visualizers show how a flow you are building will look in your org before it is deployed.
Because the agent has access to your org metadata, it can help refactor or test existing flows and reduce tech debt, and can refresh existing apps with a modern UI and brand colors.
Everything built follows your org's security settings and naming conventions, and the guests say work that used to take days or weeks can take hours.

tasks.title: Try Builder Central beta on a backlog idea and compare build time with your usual process
Audit your org for flows with tech debt that are good candidates for agent-assisted refactoring
